# Boids — Emergent Flocking

In 1986 Craig Reynolds made convincing flocks with **no leader and no plan**. Each bird, a "boid", looks only at neighbours within 60 pixels and follows three rules:

1. **Cohesion**: drift toward their centre.
2. **Alignment**: turn toward their average heading.
3. **Separation**: move away from anyone closer than 22 pixels.

Nothing in the code says "flock". The question here is how much each rule matters, and that can be measured: one number, the **order**, says how well the headings agree.

How the cells run:

- **The HTML cell is the live flock.** It reads the sliders on every frame, so drag them while it flies; nothing needs re-running.
- **JavaScript runs the same rules without drawing** and measures four settings side by side.

> ✨ The code cells were written by an AI model from prompts, and each prompt is saved in its cell: press **✨** in a cell's header to see it.

Press **Run all**.

## 1. The three weights

> Controls, 900 pixels wide, two rows of two sliders: Cohesion (toward flock centre) bound to boids_cohesion, Alignment (match headings) bound to boids_alignment and Separation (avoid crowding) bound to boids_separation, each 0 to 2, step 0.1, default 1; and Flock size bound to boids_count, 10 to 200, step 10, default 80.

Each slider multiplies one rule. 0 switches the rule off; 2 doubles it.

## 2. The live flock

> A live boids flock on a 960 by 600 canvas: each boid sees others within 60 pixels, steers toward their centre (cohesion), toward their average velocity (alignment) and away from any closer than 22 pixels (separation), each scaled by its slider in nb, read every frame. Speed stays between 1.2 and 2.6, the edges wrap, and the flock grows or shrinks to nb.boids_count. Draw the boids as small violet triangles with faint motion trails, and a line at the top with the count, the three weights and the order (how well the headings agree, 0 to 1). Dark theme.

- **One pass over the neighbours** collects all three rules: the sum of positions (cohesion), of velocities (alignment) and of pushes away (separation).
- **The speed clamp** keeps every boid moving between 1.2 and 2.6 pixels a frame, so the rules can only turn a boid, not stop it.
- **Order** is the length of the average of every boid's direction: 1 when all fly the same way, near 0 when the directions cancel out.

## 3. Measure the four experiments

> In JavaScript, run the same boids rules as the live cell without drawing for 1,500 steps under the four settings in the notes (defaults; alignment 0; cohesion 2 and separation 0; separation 2 and cohesion 0), with nb.boids_count boids, from five seeded starts each, averaging the five. Every 25 steps record the order: the length of the average heading, 1 when all fly the same way and near 0 when they point anywhere. At the end count the flocks (groups linked by boids within 60 pixels of each other) and the average distance to the nearest neighbour. Print a table and return a Vega-Lite line chart of the average order over time, one line per setting.

The four settings are the classic experiments:

- **Defaults**: all three rules at 1.
- **Alignment 0**: cohesion still pulls boids together, but nothing makes them agree on a heading.
- **Cohesion 2, separation 0**: a strong pull inward and no personal space.
- **Separation 2, cohesion 0**: personal space and no pull together.

Notes on the code:

- **`mulberry32`** is a small seeded random generator, so every setting starts from the same five flocks and the run is the same every time. One run on its own is noisy; five averaged is steadier. The live cell uses `Math.random`, so it differs a little each time.
- **Flocks** are counted with union-find: any two boids within 60 pixels join the same group.

## What the run shows

Averages of five starts, 80 boids, 1,500 steps:

| setting | order | flocks | nearest neighbour |
|---|---|---|---|
| defaults | 0.89 | 2.8 | 14.0 px |
| alignment 0 | 0.37 | 9.4 | 20.3 px |
| cohesion 2, separation 0 | 0.87 | 2.0 | 0.1 px |
| separation 2, cohesion 0 | 0.91 | 4.8 | 31.9 px |

- **The defaults make a flock.** Order climbs from 0.10 (random headings) past 0.8 by step 775 and ends at 0.89, with 80 boids in about 3 groups, 14 pixels apart.
- **Without alignment there is no flock, only a swarm.** Order creeps up as boids chase the same centres, but after 1,500 steps it is only 0.37, and the boids are split into about 9 small groups.
- **Without separation, the flock collapses.** The nearest neighbour is 0.1 pixels away: boids sit on top of each other. With 200 boids it is 0.0.
- **Separation without cohesion is a formation, not a gas.** Alignment is still on, so they all end up flying the same way (0.91), about 32 pixels apart, in about 5 loose groups.
- **None of this is written in the code.** No line says "form 3 flocks" or "fly in formation"; it comes from three rules about neighbours.

## Try this

Each of these is a prompt. Press **✨** in a cell's header to change its prompt and generate it again, or **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** at the bottom to add a new one.

- **Predict, then drag.** Before moving Alignment to 0 in the live flock, guess what the order number will do. Then drag it and watch.
- **Short-sighted birds.** Press ✨ on the JS cell and add: *"Also run the defaults with the neighbour radius at 25 and 100 pixels and compare the flock counts."*
- **Add a hawk.** Press ✨ on the HTML cell and add: *"Add one red predator that chases the nearest boid; every boid within 80 pixels of it gets a strong push away."* Watch the flock split and close up again.
- **Walls instead of wrapping.** Press ✨ on the HTML cell and add: *"Take away the wrapping: make the edges push boids back in instead."*
- **Understand the code.** Press the speech bubble (**Explain this cell**) on the JS cell and ask why every boid starts from the same seeded position.
